narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school—compared to an average around the middle of the class among accepted students—signaled to the model that you would likely struggle on the bar exam. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction, slightly pulling the prediction toward passing.

Your LSAT score of 30, well below the average of 37 among accepted students, and your lower-middle family income (a category that represents only 9% of accepted applicants) added further weight toward a negative outcome, though they were not the dominant drivers.

The school’s model does not consider gender or race in any way. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance if you retake courses, invest significant time in intensive bar exam preparation, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (248 words)
